challenger_routes.why_considered: The whole-name-in-prose rule had only ever been measured on 13 targets. Measured across all 294 path-style receipt-backed capabilities it was 270 of 294, and every one of the 24 failures was the same shape: a VERSION SIBLING. 'Run the composition cross step no bypass audit v2.' matched _v1 and _v2 identically because the trailing version token is dropped so prose without a version still names the capability; both then tie-break on the same word count and the same stem length, and iteration order picked _v1. Diagnosing that exposed a second, worse defect underneath: the identifier filter used to strip the naming prose matched ANY token containing a dot, so the sentence-final period turned the LAST WORD OF EVERY GOAL into an identifier and deleted it -- 'Run the bytes active query task generator.' lost 'generator', '... v6 candidate.' lost 'candidate', and '... audit v1.' lost the version itself, which is how a v1 sentence came to match a v2 capability.
challenger_routes.why_not_selected_or_selected: SELECTED, in three measured steps over the same 294. (1) A version the caller STATES must match the capability's own, and one they omit stays open -- 270 -> 287. (2) The version is read from ANYWHERE in the name, not only the end: reading only the trailing token wrongly rejected terminal_frontier_factorizer_v6_candidate, whose version sits mid-name, and handed the route to ..._v6; current_terminal_authority_v3_k6_v4_verifier carries two -- 287 -> 294. (3) The identifier filter now requires an INTERNAL dot, so a sentence-final period no longer deletes the last word. That third fix is what makes the first two assertable at all: three unit rules failed against the old filter, and the 294-target measurement could not see it because compile_goal can still reach the right capability through F17 retrieval while the strict predicate says no. A test written against the live corpus caught what a whole-corpus measurement missed, which is why both are kept.
